primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Biallelic GAA loss of function causes deficiency of lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase, preventing normal lysosomal glycogen degradation. Glycogen accumulates within lysosomes, damaging cardiac and skeletal muscle.
vignette: An infant has profound hypotonia, feeding difficulty, macroglossia, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Creatine kinase is elevated. Enzyme testing shows markedly reduced acid alpha-glucosidase activity.
lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
distractor_notes: McArdle disease is a skeletal-muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency that presents with exercise intolerance rather than infantile cardiomyopathy and lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency.
Von Gierke disease is a glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency causing fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, and hepatomegaly rather than primary lysosomal cardiac/skeletal-muscle glycogen accumulation.

Danon disease is an X-linked lysosomal/autophagy disorder caused by LAMP2 deficiency and can cause cardiomyopathy, but the demonstrated acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency specifically identifies Pompe disease.
Spinal muscular atrophy causes hypotonia and weakness from motor-neuron degeneration but does not cause hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with deficient lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase.
key_expl: Pompe disease is glycogen storage disease type II. Loss of lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase activity causes glycogen accumulation in lysosomes. Infantile-onset disease classically produces severe hypotonia and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, along with feeding and respiratory difficulties.
objective: Recognize infantile Pompe disease from hypotonia and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with deficient lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase activity.
